title: You Don't Understand Your Data. This Post Is the Cure.
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles argues that most schools misuse assessment and behavior data because they instinctively ask 'how do I fix this student' rather than 'how does this data reveal a flaw in the curriculum or system that will keep producing the same result.' He proposes a single reframing question, 'how is X going to make sure that all my students for the rest of time do better,' as a filter that redirects attention from individual-student intervention toward systemic curriculum change. For behavior data specifically, he recommends borrowing Social Network Analysis techniques used in crime mapping to identify the small number of socially influential students driving the majority of classroom disruption, rather than simply tracking the most visibly disruptive individuals. For exam results, he advocates using AI to model what a student with pure factual recall (but no synthesis skill) would score on a mark scheme, arguing this reveals exactly which skills, not just which content, departments are failing to teach explicitly. Throughout, Salles frames the common instinct to blame external factors (student attention spans, home circumstances, timing) as an evasion that protects the curriculum from scrutiny, arguing the discipline required is to always trace poor results back to instructional design rather than the student.
points: Proposes a single reframing question, 'how is X going to make sure that all my students for the rest of time do better,' to redirect data analysis from individual-student fixes toward systemic curriculum change.

Recommends adapting Social Network Analysis (used in crime mapping) to identify the small number of socially influential students driving most classroom disruption, rather than only tracking the most visibly disruptive individuals.

Advocates using AI to model what a student with pure factual recall but no synthesis skill would score on a mark scheme, isolating exactly which transferable skills (not just content) departments fail to teach explicitly.
Frames common explanations for poor results (attention spans, home circumstances, one-off events) as evasions that protect the curriculum from the scrutiny it actually requires.
quotes: There's something about numbers that stops people thinking. Numbers hypnotise people - either they're obsessed with a truth revealed, or they're repulsed by the idea of complexity reduced to a number.
Your mind has been conditioned to think, 'ooh, I will fill gaps', or 'I might do an intervention.' Your mind is lying to you.
The problem is the curriculum. The curriculum is the chain of events that led us here. If you don't face that fact, the problem is you.
The most valuable behaviour data are your social influencers. Map them - literally draw a map, with lines connecting each student to other students.
Understanding is memory in disguise, as Daniel Willingham tells us.
Data informs intervention: even the language is depressing. Data tells you to change the student - too little, too late, and absolutely no use to the generations following behind.
